questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of the New York State Identification Test for English Language Learners (NYSITELL)?
options: To measure each ELL's yearly growth in listening, speaking, reading, and writing and determine readiness to exit ELL status
To determine whether a newly enrolled student whose HLQ and interview indicate another language is an ELL, and at what initial level
To evaluate a newly enrolled student's home-language literacy and math skills to determine whether the student should be identified as SIFE
To screen newly enrolled students who speak a language other than English for learning disabilities before they are placed in classes
questions.why: The NYSITELL is New York's English-language identification test. A newly enrolled student takes it when the Home Language Questionnaire and the individual interview indicate a language other than English. The result determines whether the student is an ELL and, if so, the initial proficiency level that drives program placement and units of study. Measuring yearly progress and deciding exit is the job of a different test, the spring NYSESLAT.

traps.note: This describes the NYSESLAT, the annual spring test of all four modalities that sets the next year's level and determines exit. The NYSITELL is given at initial enrollment for identification.

SIFE status is determined separately, within 30 school days, using an oral interview questionnaire and, for certain languages, the MLS. The NYSITELL assesses English proficiency, not home-language literacy or math.

The NYSITELL measures English proficiency and does not screen for disabilities. Treating a home language other than English as a reason for disability screening is exactly the confusion NYS and federal guidance warn against.

questions.key: NYSITELL: given at enrollment to identify ELLs and set the initial level. NYSESLAT: given every spring to measure progress and decide exit.

questions.stimulus:
Spring results for four ELLs (both tests taken the same spring)
Student | Grade | NYSESLAT level | State ELA result
Amira (Arabic) | 3 | Transitioning | Grades 3–8 ELA: Level 3
Diego (Spanish) | 5 | Expanding | Grades 3–8 ELA: Level 3
Farida (Uzbek) | 6 | Expanding | Grades 3–8 ELA: Level 2
Jin (Mandarin) | 10 | Expanding | Regents ELA: 61
questions.stem: Based on these results, which student meets New York State criteria to exit ELL status?
options: Amira, because a Level 3 on the Grades 3–8 ELA test shows that she can meet grade-level English standards
Diego, because he scored Expanding on the NYSESLAT and Level 3 on the Grades 3–8 ELA test
Farida, because Expanding is the exit level, and the ELA test is used for school accountability, not exit
Jin, because a score of 61 on the Regents ELA exam, combined with Expanding, meets the high school route
questions.why: NYS has two exit routes. A student exits by scoring Commanding on the NYSESLAT, or by scoring Expanding AND earning Level 3 or higher on the Grades 3–8 ELA test (or 65 or higher on the Regents ELA exam). Diego meets the second route. Each of the others is missing one piece: the Expanding level (Amira), an ELA Level 3 (Farida), or a Regents score of 65 (Jin).

traps.note: The ELA-score route is open only to students who score Expanding on the NYSESLAT. Amira scored Transitioning, so her ELA Level 3 cannot substitute; she needs Expanding plus Level 3, or Commanding.
Expanding alone does not exit a student; the ELA score is part of the exit rule. Farida would also need Level 3 or higher on the Grades 3–8 ELA test, and her Level 2 falls short.
The high school route requires 65 or higher on the Regents ELA exam. Jin's 61 is below that threshold, so he remains an ELL at Expanding.

questions.key: Exit = Commanding, OR Expanding plus Grades 3–8 ELA Level 3+ or Regents ELA 65+.

questions.stimulus:
NYSESLAT modality summary: Rubina, grade 7, home language Bengali, third year of ENL services. Overall level: Transitioning.
Modality | Percent of possible points earned
Listening | 88%
Speaking | 85%
Reading | 62%
Writing | 41%
Science teacher's note: 'Rubina contributes eagerly to lab discussions, but her written conclusions are usually one or two sentences with few connecting words.'
questions.stem: Based on these data, which instructional priority would best support Rubina's English language development in her Integrated ENL science class?
options: Additional structured oral discussion, since listening and speaking are the foundation that supports all of her later literacy growth
Daily grammar and spelling worksheets during Stand-alone ENL, so that her sentence-level errors are corrected before she writes in science
Postponing extended writing in science until her reading score rises, since students need to read a genre well before they can write it
Explicit, scaffolded instruction in writing science explanations, with mentor texts and talk-to-write routines that use her oral strength
questions.why: NYSESLAT modality data show where a student's English is uneven. Rubina's listening and speaking are far ahead of her reading and especially her writing, and the teacher's note confirms short, unconnected written conclusions. The best response targets the weakest modality within grade-level content and uses her oral strength as a bridge: talk-to-write routines let her rehearse ideas aloud, and mentor texts and frames help her produce extended, cohesive explanations.

traps.note: Listening and speaking are already Rubina's strongest modalities. This option ignores what the profile shows (writing is the weakest area) and spends instructional time on a strength.

Decontextualized grammar worksheets do not teach her to organize and connect ideas in a science explanation. The note shows a discourse-level need (extended, connected writing), not just sentence-level errors.
Reading and writing develop together, and delaying writing withholds the practice she most needs. Waiting until one skill is 'ready' is a wait-until-proficient approach that slows growth.

questions.key: Use NYSESLAT modality patterns to target the weakest modality in content, with the stronger modalities as a bridge.

questions.stem: A first-grade ELL whose home language is Polish scores Expanding on the spring NYSESLAT. Her father asks the ENL teacher whether she will exit ELL status before second grade. Which response is most accurate?
options: Yes. A student who scores Expanding exits ELL status and then receives two years of former-ELL support.
Not yet. She will take the NYSITELL again in the fall to confirm that her English is now proficient.
Not yet. Without a Grades 3–8 ELA score, a first grader can exit only by scoring Commanding on the NYSESLAT.
It depends. Her classroom teacher will decide in the fall, based on her report card and her reading level.
questions.why: The Expanding route to exit requires Level 3 or higher on the Grades 3–8 ELA test, which students in kindergarten through grade 2 do not take. A first grader who scores Expanding therefore remains an ELL, receiving Expanding-level services (180 minutes per week of Integrated ENL), and can exit by scoring Commanding on a later NYSESLAT. Exit is not a teacher's discretionary call, and it is not decided by a NYSITELL retest.

traps.note: Expanding is not an exit level by itself. It must be paired with Level 3+ on the Grades 3–8 ELA test or 65+ on the Regents ELA exam, and a first grader has neither.
The NYSITELL is used at initial enrollment for identification; it is not readministered to confirm exit. Exit is determined by the NYSESLAT (with the ELA score where applicable).
Exit from ELL status follows state test criteria, not teacher discretion or report card grades. Classroom evidence informs instruction, but it does not decide exit.

questions.key: K–2 ELLs have no Grades 3–8 ELA score, so they exit only by scoring Commanding on the NYSESLAT.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the New York State English as a Second Language Achievement Test (NYSESLAT) is accurate?
options: It is given each spring to ELLs in grades K–12 and assesses listening, speaking, reading, and writing to set proficiency levels.
It is given once, at initial enrollment, to determine whether a student whose home language is not English needs ENL services.
It is given each spring to all students in grades 3–8 and measures English reading and writing against grade-level ELA standards.
It is given each fall to ELLs and measures their knowledge of math, science, and social studies content in the home language.
questions.why: The NYSESLAT is the annual spring assessment of English proficiency for identified ELLs in grades K–12, and it covers all four modalities: listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Its result places the student at one of five levels (Entering, Emerging, Transitioning, Expanding, Commanding), which sets the next year's units of study and, with the exit criteria, determines whether the student exits. The identification test given at enrollment is a different test, the NYSITELL.

traps.note: This describes the NYSITELL, the identification test given at enrollment. The NYSESLAT is the annual measure for students who have already been identified as ELLs.
This describes the Grades 3–8 ELA test, which all students take. The NYSESLAT is given only to ELLs and measures English proficiency in four modalities, not grade-level ELA achievement.
The NYSESLAT is a spring test of English language proficiency, not a fall content test in the home language. Content knowledge is measured by state content tests, which ELLs take with accommodations.

questions.key: NYSESLAT: every spring, ELLs only, all four modalities, five levels; it drives next year's services and exit decisions.

questions.stem: A grade 6 student scored Commanding on the NYSESLAT last spring. In September, the ENL teacher is planning the student's program for grade 7. Which plan is consistent with NYS requirements?
options: No further ENL services or NYSESLAT testing, since a Commanding score means the student is treated like any general education student
Continued ENL support and ELL testing accommodations for four years, matching the time former ELLs may remain in the ELL subgroup
Continued ENL support of 90 minutes per week and ELL testing accommodations for two years, with no further NYSESLAT testing
Continued ENL support of 180 minutes per week, with one more NYSESLAT next spring to confirm that the Commanding score holds
questions.why: A Commanding score makes the student a former ELL. Under CR Part 154, former ELLs in grades K–8 receive 90 minutes per week of Integrated ENL (or other approved former-ELL services) for two years, and they keep ELL testing accommodations for two years after exit. They no longer take the NYSESLAT. The four-year figure belongs to ESSA, which lets states count former ELs in the EL subgroup for up to four years for accountability; it is not a service requirement.

traps.note: Exiting ends ELL status, not support. Former ELLs receive two years of continued ENL support and keep ELL testing accommodations for two years.

Four years is ESSA's accountability rule: states may keep former ELs in the EL subgroup for up to four years when reporting results. NYS services and testing accommodations for former ELLs last two years.
180 minutes per week is the Transitioning/Expanding requirement, and former ELLs do not retake the NYSESLAT. A Commanding score ends NYSESLAT testing.

questions.key: Former ELLs: 2 years of support (90 min/week in K–8) plus testing accommodations. ESSA's 4 years concerns accountability reporting only.

questions.stem: A grade 4 student from Ukraine who attended an English-medium international school in Kyiv enrolls in a Buffalo elementary school. Her HLQ and interview indicate that Ukrainian is spoken at home, so she takes the NYSITELL, and she scores Commanding. Which statement best describes her status?
options: She is not identified as an ELL, so she does not receive ENL services or take the NYSESLAT in the spring.
She is identified as a former ELL and receives two years of continued ENL support and testing accommodations.
She is identified as an ELL at the Expanding level until the spring NYSESLAT confirms her English proficiency.
She is identified as an ELL because her HLQ shows a home language other than English, and she is served until she exits.
questions.why: Identification has two steps. The HLQ and interview decide whether a student needs to take the NYSITELL, and the NYSITELL result decides ELL status. A student who scores Commanding on the NYSITELL is not an ELL. Because she was never identified, she is not a 'former ELL' either; that status, with its two years of continued support and accommodations, belongs to students who were identified as ELLs and later exited.

traps.note: Former-ELL status applies to students who were identified as ELLs and later met exit criteria. A student who scores Commanding on the NYSITELL was never an ELL, so she is not a former ELL.
There is no provisional ELL placement while waiting for the NYSESLAT. A Commanding score on the NYSITELL means the student is not an ELL, so no ENL level is assigned.
The HLQ and interview determine only whether the student must take the NYSITELL. ELL status depends on the NYSITELL result, not on the home language alone.

questions.key: Commanding on the NYSITELL means not an ELL (and not a former ELL). A non-English home language alone doesn't make a student an ELL.

questions.stimulus:
Spring NYSESLAT results for two grade 4 ELLs, both Transitioning overall (percent of possible points earned in each modality)
Modality | Lucía (Spanish) | Tenzin (Tibetan)
Listening | 58% | 90%
Speaking | 52% | 87%
Reading | 81% | 55%
Writing | 77% | 49%
questions.stem: The ENL teacher is planning small-group instruction for these two students. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Because both students are Transitioning, they should receive the same small-group instruction and the same set of scaffolds.
Lucía most needs structured academic talk and Tenzin most needs targeted literacy support, both within shared grade-level content.
Tenzin's low reading and writing scores, despite his strong oral English, suggest a learning disability that warrants a referral.
Lucía's low listening and speaking scores suggest that she is still in a silent period and should not yet be expected to speak.
questions.why: A single overall NYSESLAT level can hide very different modality profiles. Lucía's reading and writing are well ahead of her listening and speaking, so she needs structured academic conversation, with frames, rehearsal, and interaction, to build oral output. Tenzin's strong oral English and weaker literacy call for targeted reading and writing instruction. Modality data let the teacher differentiate within the same grade-level content instead of treating one level as one profile.

traps.note: The same overall level can come from very different modality profiles. Treating 'Transitioning' as one profile ignores that these two students' strengths and needs are nearly opposite.
Literacy lagging behind oral language is a common second-language pattern, especially for students with less prior literacy instruction. Uneven modality scores alone are not evidence of a disability.
The silent period describes beginners at the earliest stage of acquisition. Lucía reads and writes at a fairly high level; she needs structured opportunities for oral output, not a pass on speaking.

questions.key: One overall NYSESLAT level can mask different modality profiles; use modality data to target each student's need.

questions.stem: In September, a grade 8 Integrated ENL co-teaching team receives the previous spring's NYSESLAT results. The ELA teacher proposes using each student's overall NYSESLAT level as the sole basis for assigning reading groups for the entire year. Which response by the ENL teacher reflects the soundest use of the data?
options: Agree, since the NYSESLAT is the state's official measure of English proficiency and is more reliable than classroom assessments
Suggest setting the NYSESLAT results aside, since a test given months earlier cannot tell teachers anything useful about students now
Suggest placing all of the ELLs in one reading group, so that the ENL teacher can address their shared language needs together
Suggest combining the NYSESLAT data with current classroom reading assessments and revisiting the groups as students progress
questions.why: The NYSESLAT is a valid annual measure of English proficiency, and its overall level and modality pattern are a useful starting point. However, it was given months earlier and was not designed to be the sole basis for instructional grouping. The Blueprint calls for diverse and valid assessments, so teachers should triangulate NYSESLAT data with current classroom evidence (running records, writing samples, formative checks) and regroup flexibly as students grow.

traps.note: The NYSESLAT is the official proficiency measure, but it is a single annual snapshot of English proficiency, not a diagnostic reading assessment. Using it as the only basis for year-long groups ignores current evidence and growth.
Fixating on the time lag throws away useful information. Last spring's overall level and modality pattern are a valid starting point; they just need to be updated with current classroom data.
ELLs at different levels have different needs, and a single 'ELL group' ignores those differences. It can also isolate ELLs from peers who model grade-level reading.

questions.key: Treat the NYSESLAT as one data point; combine it with current classroom evidence and regroup flexibly.

questions.stem: A student whose HLQ indicates that Nepali is spoken at home enrolls in a Queens elementary school for the first time on October 1. Under CR Part 154, by when must the school complete the ELL identification process, including the NYSITELL if it is required?
options: Within 10 school days of the student's initial enrollment
Within 30 school days of the student's initial enrollment
Within 45 school days of the student's initial enrollment
Before the spring NYSESLAT administration in that school year
questions.why: CR Part 154 requires the full identification process (the HLQ, an individual interview in English and the home language, and the NYSITELL if indicated) to be completed within 10 school days of initial enrollment. Parents must then be notified of the result within 5 school days of the determination, in their preferred language. The other numbers belong to different processes: 30 school days for SIFE determination and 45 school days for requesting a re-identification review.

traps.note: Thirty school days is the window for determining SIFE status, which follows ELL identification. ELL identification itself must be completed within 10 school days.

Forty-five school days is the window in which a parent, a teacher (with parent consent), or the student (if 18 or older) may request a re-identification review. It is not the deadline for initial identification.
Identification cannot wait months, because services depend on it. The NYSESLAT measures the progress of students already identified, so it plays no part in initial identification.

questions.key: Identification: 10 school days. Parent notice: within 5 school days after. SIFE: 30 school days. Re-identification request: 45 school days.

questions.stem: A grade 3 student with an IEP transfers into a NYS district from out of state. The HLQ and interview indicate that Karen is the primary language spoken at home. Which step is consistent with CR Part 154 before the student is given the NYSITELL?
options: The Committee on Special Education reviews the IEP and decides on its own whether the student will take the NYSITELL.
The student is exempt from the NYSITELL, since the IEP already documents the student's needs and the services required.
A Language Proficiency Team decides whether the student takes the NYSITELL and sends its recommendation to the superintendent.
The student takes the NYSITELL right away with IEP accommodations, and a team reviews the results if the student scores at the Entering level.
questions.why: For a newly enrolled student with an IEP, NYS requires a Language Proficiency Team (LPT) to review evidence such as the student's history, language use, and disability, and to decide whether the student should take the NYSITELL. The LPT's recommendation goes to the superintendent. This step keeps a disability from being mistaken for limited English proficiency, or the reverse. It is not a CSE decision, and an IEP does not exempt the student from identification.

traps.note: The CSE develops IEPs, but the decision about giving the NYSITELL to a newly enrolled student with an IEP belongs to the Language Proficiency Team, whose recommendation goes to the superintendent.
An IEP does not exempt a student from ELL identification. Language needs and disability needs are separate questions, and a student can be both an ELL and a student with a disability.

For students with IEPs, the LPT review comes before the decision to give the NYSITELL, not after a low score. The safeguard exists so that a disability is not mistaken for limited English proficiency, or the reverse.

questions.key: Newly enrolled student with an IEP: the LPT decides whether to give the NYSITELL and sends its recommendation to the superintendent.

questions.stem: A grade 5 student from Guatemala whose home language is K'iche' enrolls in a NYS school for the first time in January and is identified as an ELL at the Entering level. Which statement about her spring state testing is accurate?
options: She is exempt from all state tests this year, since she has attended school in the United States for less than one year.
She takes the Grade 5 ELA test with a K'iche' bilingual glossary, and the reading passages may be translated for her orally.
She takes the Grade 5 ELA test in place of the NYSESLAT, since a student does not take two state English tests in one year.
She may be exempted once from the Grade 5 ELA test and take the NYSESLAT, but she takes the math test with accommodations.
questions.why: NYS allows ELLs in their first year in U.S. schools to be exempted one time from the Grades 3–8 ELA test; the NYSESLAT serves as their English assessment that year. The exemption does not extend to math, which she takes with ELL accommodations such as extended time, a separate location, or oral translation, since K'iche' is a lower-incidence language. Translation and glossary supports never apply to ELA tests.

traps.note: The first-year exemption covers the Grades 3–8 ELA test, not every state test. She still takes the state math test, with ELL accommodations.
None of the translation or glossary supports apply to ELA tests, because ELA tests measure English itself. Glossaries and oral translation are for math, science, and social studies tests.
This reverses the policy. ELLs take the NYSESLAT every year; the first-year provision exempts her from the ELA test, not from the NYSESLAT.

questions.key: First-year ELLs get a one-time exemption from the Grades 3–8 ELA test only. They take the NYSESLAT, and math with accommodations.

questions.stimulus:
NYSESLAT history: Yusuf, home language Urdu, identified as an ELL in grade 2 and now in grade 9 (eighth year of ENL services). Modality columns show the teacher's summary of relative performance.
Grade | Overall level | Listening | Speaking | Reading | Writing
5 | Transitioning | High | High | Low | Low
6 | Expanding | High | High | Middle | Low
7 | Expanding | High | High | Middle | Low
8 | Expanding | High | High | Middle | Low
Grade 8 ELA test: Level 2.
ENL teacher's note: 'Socially fluent and confident in discussion; avoids extended reading; essays are short and informal in tone.'
questions.stem: Which interpretation of Yusuf's data is most accurate and most useful for planning?
options: He is a Long-Term ELL with strong conversational English but stalled academic reading and writing, who needs explicit academic literacy instruction.
His three-year plateau despite fluent conversational English suggests a learning disability, so he should be referred to the CSE for an evaluation.
His strong listening and speaking show that he has developed CALP, so his ENL services are mainly a formality until he passes the ELA test.
He is a Developing ELL whose results show steady growth, so his current program should continue unchanged until he meets the exit criteria.
questions.why: Having completed more than six years of ELL services, Yusuf is a Long-Term ELL. His profile is a classic one: high listening and speaking (BICS) with stalled reading and writing (CALP), three straight years at Expanding, and an ELA Level 2 that keeps him from exiting. The data call for explicit, content-based academic literacy instruction (complex texts with scaffolds, academic vocabulary, and genre-based writing) rather than a referral or more of the same.

traps.note: A plateau in academic literacy alongside strong oral English is the typical Long-Term ELL profile and does not by itself suggest a disability. The first step is targeted academic literacy instruction, with close monitoring of its effect.
Fluent listening and speaking in social settings reflect BICS. CALP is the academic language of complex reading and writing, which is exactly where Yusuf is stuck.
Developing ELLs have 4–6 years of service; Yusuf is in his eighth year, which makes him a Long-Term ELL. His results have also been flat for three years, not rising, so his program needs to change.

questions.key: Long-Term ELL profile: strong oral English, stalled academic literacy. Respond with explicit academic literacy instruction, not a referral.

questions.stimulus:
Schoolwide NYSESLAT summary for ELLs in grades 6–8 (average percent of possible points earned)
Grade | Listening | Speaking | Reading | Writing
6 | 78% | 74% | 61% | 44%
7 | 80% | 77% | 63% | 46%
8 | 81% | 79% | 60% | 43%
questions.stem: A middle school's ENL coordinator reviews this summary with the school leadership team. Which next step is the most appropriate use of these data?
options: Add a daily Stand-alone ENL period of grammar drills for all ELLs, so that the errors that lower their writing scores are corrected
Shift ENL instruction toward listening and speaking, since oral language underlies every other modality and improves most quickly
Plan professional learning and co-planning time for ENL and content teachers on scaffolding academic writing in every subject
Share each ELL's writing score with content teachers so that they can reduce the amount of writing they require from ELLs
questions.why: When the same gap appears at every grade (here, writing far below the other modalities), it signals a program-level need rather than individual difficulties. Because academic writing develops through meaningful use across subjects, the most effective response builds capacity schoolwide: ENL and content teachers co-plan scaffolds such as mentor texts, sentence frames, and genre instruction. This reflects the Blueprint principles that every teacher is a teacher of ELLs and that schools should leverage ESOL expertise.

traps.note: Grammar drills in isolation do not teach students to organize and develop academic writing in the content areas. The data reveal a writing need, but the fix must be meaningful, content-based writing instruction.
Listening and speaking are the strongest modalities at every grade. Shifting time toward them ignores the clear pattern in the data: writing is the schoolwide gap.
Reducing writing demands lowers expectations and denies ELLs the practice they need. Low writing scores call for more scaffolded writing, not less writing.

questions.key: A schoolwide NYSESLAT pattern calls for a schoolwide response, such as co-planning and professional learning on the weak modality.

questions.stimulus:
Item 4 from a grade 6 teacher-made unit test on ratios:
'Notwithstanding the inclement weather that had persisted throughout the preceding week, the members of the Ridgewood Middle School environmental club resolved to proceed with their annual park restoration endeavor. If the club's 24 members were apportioned such that the ratio of seventh graders to eighth graders was 3:1, how many eighth graders participated?'
Result: Most Emerging and Transitioning ELLs answered incorrectly, although most of them had correctly solved a similar ratio problem the day before during a class activity that used a table and pictures.
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the problem with using this item to assess the ELLs' understanding of ratios?
options: The item is unreliable, since students would probably earn different scores if they took the same test again on another day.
The item is culturally biased, since students from other countries are unlikely to be familiar with school environmental clubs.
The item's complex vocabulary and syntax add language demands unrelated to ratios, which weakens the validity of ELLs' scores.
The item is appropriate for ELLs, since grade 6 students are expected to read complex academic text in every content area.
questions.why: Validity asks whether scores reflect the construct the test is meant to measure. This item buries a simple ratio problem in low-frequency words ('notwithstanding,' 'apportioned') and long clauses, so an ELL's wrong answer may reflect English reading proficiency rather than ratio reasoning. This is called construct-irrelevant variance, and the class evidence confirms it. Reducing the linguistic load while keeping the same math would make the item a more valid measure of ratios.

traps.note: Reliability is about consistency of scores, and nothing in the data suggests inconsistency. The problem is that the item measures the wrong thing for these students, which is a validity issue.

This latches onto the story's setting and assumes what students from other countries know. The evidence (correct answers to a similar problem presented with a table and pictures) points to the item's language, not its topic.
Reading complex text is a legitimate goal, but a ratio test is meant to measure ratio reasoning. When reading load decides the score, the test measures English proficiency instead of math.

questions.key: Unneeded language load on a content test measures English, not content. That is a validity problem.

questions.stem: At the end of a grade 3 Integrated ENL lesson on animal habitats, students complete an exit ticket with a picture prompt and the frame 'A ___ lives in the ___ because ___.' That afternoon, the co-teachers sort the tickets to form small groups and choose scaffolds for the next day's lesson. Which of the following best describes this use of the exit tickets?
options: Summative assessment, because it measures what students learned at the end of the lesson
Norm-referenced assessment, because students' responses are compared to sort them into groups
Performance assessment, because students produce a response instead of selecting an answer
Formative assessment, because the results are used to adjust the instruction that follows
questions.why: Formative vs. summative depends on how results are used, not on when the task happens. Because the teachers use the exit tickets to form groups and plan scaffolds for the next day, this is formative assessment, or assessment for learning. Summative assessment evaluates learning at the end of a unit or period, usually for a grade or a report.

traps.note: Timing doesn't define the type; purpose does. A task at the end of a lesson is still formative when its results shape the next lesson, while summative assessment evaluates learning at the end of a unit or course.
Norm-referenced tests rank students against a norm group. Sorting tickets by what students need next is diagnostic grouping, not comparison with a norm group.
Students do produce a response, but that describes the task's format, not how the results are used. What defines this assessment is that it guides the next day's teaching.

questions.key: Formative: results are used to adjust instruction. Summative: results are used to evaluate learning at the end of a unit or course.

questions.stimulus:
Two grade 10 English teachers scored the same three ELL argument essays on the department's 4-point rubric without discussing it beforehand.
Essay | Teacher 1 | Teacher 2
Essay A | 4 | 2
Essay B | 3 | 1
Essay C | 2 | 4
questions.stem: Which step would most directly address the problem these scores reveal?
options: Have the teachers score a set of anchor papers together, discuss the rubric criteria, and practice until their scores agree
Average the two teachers' scores for each essay, so that every student receives a balanced and fair final grade
Replace the essay with a multiple-choice test on argument writing, since selected-response items can be scored consistently by machine
Revise the essay prompt so that it is more closely aligned with the grade 10 standards for writing arguments
questions.why: When the same essays receive very different scores from two raters, the problem is inter-rater reliability, which is the consistency of scoring. The standard fix is calibration: raters score anchor papers together, discuss how each rubric criterion applies, and practice until their scores converge. This matters especially for ELLs, because untrained raters may react very differently to developing language control in essays with similar ideas.

traps.note: Averaging produces a number, but it hides the inconsistency instead of fixing it. The next set of essays would be scored just as unpredictably.
Multiple-choice items are scored consistently, but they cannot show whether a student can write an argument. This trades a reliability problem for a validity problem.
Alignment with the standards is a validity concern. The problem in the data is that two raters scoring the same essays disagree, which is a scoring-consistency (reliability) problem.

questions.key: Different scores from different raters signal a reliability problem. Fix it with clear rubrics, anchor papers, and calibration.

questions.stem: A score report states that a grade 4 student 'scored at the 38th percentile compared with a national sample of fourth graders.' This kind of score interpretation is characteristic of which type of assessment?
options: A criterion-referenced test, which reports how well a student has mastered a defined set of standards
A formative assessment, which provides results that teachers use to adjust day-to-day instruction
A performance assessment, which reports how well a student completes a complex, real-world task
A norm-referenced test, which reports how a student's performance compares with that of a norm group
questions.why: Percentile ranks are the hallmark of norm-referenced tests: they show how a student compares with a norm group, not what the student can do. Criterion-referenced tests compare performance with a fixed standard or cut score, as proficiency levels do. With ELLs, teachers should also ask whether the norm group included students like them; if it did not, the comparison may be misleading.

traps.note: Criterion-referenced tests compare performance with a fixed standard or cut score, such as a proficiency level. A percentile compares the student with other test takers.
Formative describes how results are used in the classroom. A percentile rank against a national sample comes from a standardized norm-referenced test, not a classroom check.
Performance assessment describes a task format (doing or producing something). The percentile wording describes how the score is interpreted: by comparison with a norm group.

questions.key: A percentile rank means norm-referenced (comparison with peers). A level based on a fixed standard means criterion-referenced.

questions.stimulus: A grade 5 teacher-made reading quiz uses a passage about a family preparing Thanksgiving dinner. Question 3 asks: 'Why did Grandma make the cranberry sauce the night before?' The answer depends on knowing that the dish must chill and set before it is served, which the passage never states.
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the main problem with Question 3 as a measure of reading comprehension for some students in the class, including several recently arrived ELLs?
options: It is culturally biased, since a correct answer depends on background knowledge that the passage does not provide.
It has low reliability, since students might give different answers if they took the same quiz on a different day.
It is a recall question rather than an inference question, so it does not measure higher-order comprehension.
It uses difficult vocabulary, so it should be replaced with a question about the passage that uses simpler words.
questions.why: An item is biased when some students' scores depend on something other than the skill being measured. Here, the answer depends on culturally specific knowledge (how cranberry sauce is prepared) that the passage never provides, so students who did not grow up with this tradition can miss it even if they understood the text. The fix is to ask about information or inferences the text supports, not to make the item easier.

traps.note: Nothing suggests scores would change from day to day; a student lacking the cultural knowledge would miss the item every time. The problem is systematic: the item measures cultural experience, which is bias.
The question does call for an inference, but one that rests on outside cultural knowledge rather than on the text. Labeling the question type misses why it is unfair.
The barrier is culture-specific knowledge, not vocabulary, so simpler words would not fix it. Replacing a challenging question with an easier one also lowers rigor instead of making the item fair.

questions.key: An item that requires culture-specific knowledge the text doesn't supply is biased; it measures experience, not the target skill.

questions.stem: A grade 4 class has finished a science unit on simple circuits. The ENL teacher and the classroom teacher want an assessment that lets two Emerging-level ELLs show what they understand about how a circuit works. Which assessment would provide the most valid evidence of their content learning?
options: A written short-answer test that asks students to explain in complete paragraphs why some circuits light a bulb and others do not
A task in which students build a working circuit, then label a diagram and explain it orally using a word bank and sentence frames
A matching quiz in which students connect circuit vocabulary such as battery, wire, and switch to written English definitions
An exemption from the unit assessment, with a grade based on participation until the students' English allows a fair test
questions.why: A performance assessment asks students to demonstrate knowledge by doing something, here building a working circuit, so the evidence of understanding does not depend on extended English writing. Adding a labeled diagram and an oral explanation with a word bank and frames lets Emerging students show content understanding at their language level while still using academic language. The content construct stays intact, and construct-irrelevant language demands are kept low.

traps.note: Paragraph-length written explanations in English are well beyond what Emerging students can produce independently, so the scores would mainly reflect English writing rather than knowledge of circuits.
Matching words to definitions measures vocabulary recall in isolation. A student could match 'switch' to its definition without understanding how a circuit works.
Exempting ELLs from assessment denies them, and their teachers, evidence of learning and signals lower expectations. The goal is valid assessment with supports, not removal.

questions.key: Performance tasks with visuals and supported oral or written explanation give valid evidence of ELLs' content learning.

questions.stem: An ENL teacher wants to document a grade 7 Transitioning student's growth in writing over the school year and share it with the student and family at conferences. Which approach best reflects the purpose of portfolio assessment?
options: Keeping every assignment the student completes in a folder, so the family can see the full amount of work done during the year
Collecting the student's highest-scoring tests from each marking period, so the family can see the student's best performance
Comparing the student's writing samples with those of classmates, so the family can see where the student ranks in the class
Selecting dated writing samples tied to set goals, scored with one consistent rubric and paired with the student's reflections
questions.why: A portfolio is a purposeful, systematic collection of student work that shows growth over time toward stated goals. Its power comes from selection criteria, dated samples, consistent scoring (often with a rubric), and student self-reflection, which together let the student, family, and teachers see progress that a single test score can hide. For ELLs, portfolios can also include drafts, oral recordings, and work that draws on the home language.

traps.note: A folder of everything has no selection criteria or goals, so growth is hard to see. A portfolio is a purposeful, selective collection.
A best-work collection can be one kind of portfolio, but showing only peak test scores hides the growth over time that this teacher wants to document.
Ranking against classmates turns the portfolio into a norm-referenced comparison. A portfolio compares the student with her own earlier work and with her goals.

questions.key: A portfolio is purposeful: dated samples, goals or criteria, a consistent rubric, and student reflection that show growth over time.

questions.stem: An ENL teacher wants a rubric for grade 6 argument essays that gives students separate feedback on claim and evidence, organization, and language use, so that each student can see which area to work on next. Which type of rubric best fits this purpose?
options: An analytic rubric, which scores each criterion separately on its own scale of performance levels
A holistic rubric, which assigns one overall score based on the general quality of the whole essay
A checklist, which records whether each required element of the essay is present or absent
A norm-referenced scale, which scores each essay by comparing it with the other essays in the class
questions.why: An analytic rubric breaks performance into separate criteria (such as claim and evidence, organization, and language use), each with its own performance levels. That produces diagnostic feedback and lets teachers see, for instance, that an ELL's reasoning is strong while language control is still developing. A holistic rubric gives one overall score, which is faster but less useful for next steps. Separate criteria also help keep content and language scores distinct.

traps.note: A holistic rubric yields one overall score. It is efficient, but it cannot show a student that, for example, her evidence is strong while her organization needs work.
A checklist shows whether elements are present, but not how well each one is done. It lacks the performance levels needed for feedback on quality.
Comparing essays with one another ranks students instead of describing performance against criteria, so it gives no specific guidance on what to improve.

questions.key: Analytic rubric: a separate score for each criterion (diagnostic). Holistic rubric: one overall score.

questions.stimulus:
Grade 8 science lab report rubric (20 points)
Criterion | Points
Uses correct spelling and capitalization | 6
Report is neat and typed | 4
Includes all required section headings | 4
Explains whether the data support the hypothesis, citing evidence | 6
Lesson objective: Students will evaluate whether experimental data support a hypothesis, citing evidence.
questions.stem: What is the most significant concern about this rubric as a measure of the lesson objective?
options: Its criteria lack descriptors for each performance level, so two teachers could award different points to the same report.
Fourteen of its 20 points reward conventions and format, so scores mainly reflect skills other than the lesson objective.
It lacks a separate criterion for academic science vocabulary, which ELLs need to develop through their lab writing.
It requires too many section headings, so ELLs should be allowed to skip the headings and turn in a shorter report.
questions.why: A rubric is valid for a lesson when its criteria and their weighting match the learning target. Here, 14 of 20 points go to spelling, neatness, and headings, while evaluating data against a hypothesis, the actual objective, earns only 6. An ELL who reasons well but is still developing conventions could score poorly, while a student with tidy reports and weak reasoning could score well. Descriptors or a vocabulary criterion may help, but the primary fix is reweighting the rubric toward the objective.

traps.note: Missing level descriptors is a real reliability concern, but even perfectly consistent scoring of this rubric would still mostly measure spelling, neatness, and format rather than the objective.
A vocabulary criterion could support a language objective, but it leaves the main flaw untouched: most of the points still have nothing to do with evaluating data.
Exempting ELLs from parts of the task lowers expectations and does nothing about the rubric's misalignment with the objective.

questions.key: Rubric criteria and points must match the objective; heavy weighting on conventions or format undermines validity.

questions.stem: A grade 2 ENL teacher wants her Emerging-level students to begin assessing their own progress toward each lesson's language objective. Which approach is most appropriate for these students?
options: Asking students to write a paragraph in English at the end of each week describing what they learned and what is still hard
Waiting to introduce self-assessment until students reach the Expanding level and can judge the quality of their own work
Using a short can-do checklist with icons tied to the objective, modeled by the teacher and revisited regularly to set goals
Asking students to rate their overall understanding on a scale of 1 to 10 at the end of each lesson, without specific criteria
questions.why: Self-assessment builds metacognition and ownership when it is tied to clear, specific objectives and matched to students' language level. For Emerging second graders, a can-do checklist with icons (for example, 'I can tell my partner where an animal lives') makes the criteria comprehensible. Teacher modeling and regular use teach students how to judge their progress and set the next goal.

traps.note: An independent written reflection paragraph in English is beyond what most Emerging second graders can produce, so the task would measure writing rather than self-awareness.
Students at every level can self-assess when the criteria are made comprehensible. Waiting until Expanding withholds a powerful learning tool for years.
A rating scale is a form of self-assessment, but without criteria tied to the objective, students have no basis for judging their progress or setting goals.

questions.key: Self-assessment works at every level when the criteria are specific, visual, modeled, and matched to the students' language level.

questions.stem: In a grade 9 Integrated ENL English class, students at the Transitioning and Expanding levels will give each other feedback on drafts of an argument essay. Which plan is most likely to make the peer assessment productive?
options: Pair each ELL with a native English speaker, who will correct the grammar and spelling errors in the ELL's draft before it is turned in
Have students read each other's drafts and assign a score from 1 to 4, which the teacher then averages into each draft's final grade
Ask students to exchange drafts and write whatever suggestions they think will help, so that the feedback reflects real reader response
Give students a short checklist drawn from the rubric, model feedback on a sample draft, and provide sentence frames for their comments
questions.why: Peer assessment works when students understand the criteria and have the language to give feedback. A checklist drawn from the rubric focuses attention on what matters (claim, evidence, reasoning); modeling with a sample draft shows what useful feedback looks like; and frames such as 'Your claim is clear because…' or 'You could add evidence about…' give ELLs the academic language to comment respectfully and specifically.

traps.note: This turns peer review into proofreading and makes the ELL a passive recipient. It focuses on surface errors instead of the argument's claim, evidence, and reasoning.
Untrained peer scores are not reliable enough to count toward grades, and grading pressure undermines honest, useful feedback.
Genuine reader response has value, but without criteria and modeling, feedback tends to be vague ('Good job!'), and ELLs may lack the language to give specific comments.

questions.key: Productive peer assessment needs rubric-based criteria, teacher modeling, and sentence frames for giving feedback.

questions.stem: During a grade 5 Integrated ENL math lesson, the teacher wants to check quickly whether every student, including several Entering and Emerging ELLs, understands how to compare fractions before moving on. Which strategy would give the teacher the most useful information?
options: Having every student show an answer to a fraction comparison on a mini whiteboard, using a model or a symbol
Asking the class 'Does everyone understand?' and moving on to the next part of the lesson when most students nod
Calling on two or three volunteers to come to the board and explain their reasoning aloud to the rest of the class
Noting which students look confused and waiting for the end-of-unit test to confirm who has mastered the skill
questions.why: Effective formative checks gather evidence from every student, in a form that doesn't depend heavily on English. Mini whiteboards let all students show an answer at once, with a drawing, a number line, or a symbol (<, >), so the teacher can see immediately who needs reteaching. Yes/no questions and volunteers give an incomplete picture, especially of ELLs.

traps.note: A yes/no comprehension question yields almost no evidence. Students may nod to be polite or to avoid attention, so the teacher cannot tell who actually understands.
Volunteers' explanations are useful, but they show only what the most confident students know, and the ELLs who most need support are the least likely to volunteer.
The unit test is summative and comes too late to adjust today's instruction, and appearances are unreliable evidence. The teacher needs formative evidence from every student now.

questions.key: Check understanding with responses from every student (whiteboards, response cards), not yes/no questions or volunteers.

questions.stimulus: A middle school uses a 40-item timed vocabulary-definition test to decide which ELLs may enroll in an advanced literature elective. Students who take the test twice, a week apart, earn nearly identical scores. However, several ELLs with low scores have written insightful, well-supported literary analyses in class, and some high scorers struggle to interpret texts.
questions.stem: Which statement best describes this test as a basis for the placement decision?
options: It is valid but not reliable, since the students' classroom work does not match their test scores.
It is valid and reliable, since consistent scores show that it accurately measures each student's readiness for literature.
It is reliable but not valid, since its consistent scores do not reflect the skills that the elective requires.
It is neither valid nor reliable, since a timed test cannot produce consistent results for ELLs.
questions.why: Reliability is consistency: nearly identical scores a week apart show that the test is reliable. Validity is whether scores support the intended use, and vocabulary-definition recall does not predict the literary analysis the elective requires, as the classroom evidence shows. A test can be reliable without being valid, but it cannot be valid without being reliable. Using this test as a gatekeeper also raises an equity concern, since it may keep capable ELLs out of advanced coursework.

traps.note: The mismatch with classwork is a validity problem, not unreliability. Scores a week apart were nearly identical, so the test is consistent.
Consistency (reliability) is not the same as measuring the right thing (validity). A test can rank students the same way every time and still measure the wrong skill.
The data show the test is consistent, so it is reliable. The timed format may add pressure, but the stimulus directly contradicts the claim that the results are inconsistent.

questions.key: Reliable means consistent; valid means it measures what the decision requires. A test can be reliable yet invalid.

questions.stem: A school psychologist proposes using a nationally norm-referenced English reading test to help decide whether a grade 3 ELL at the Emerging level has a reading disability. The test's norm group consisted of monolingual English-speaking third graders. Which concern should the ENL teacher raise first?
options: The test should be given with extended time, since ELLs typically need more time to process text that is written in English.
The test's norms do not represent ELLs, so a low score may reflect English proficiency rather than a reading disability.
The test should be translated orally into the home language, so the student can understand each item as it is read.
The test should be replaced by the NYSESLAT, since it is the state's official measure of ELLs' reading ability.
questions.why: Norm-referenced scores are meaningful only when the student resembles the norm group. Comparing an Emerging ELL with monolingual English speakers measures English proficiency as much as reading ability, so a low percentile cannot distinguish a disability from typical second-language development. IDEA requires evaluations in the child's native language and bars identifying a disability that is really the result of limited English proficiency; extended time or ad hoc translation cannot repair norms built on a different population.

traps.note: Extended time may reduce one barrier, but the student is still being compared with a norm group unlike her, so the percentile still cannot separate language from disability.
On-the-spot translation changes the test, so the published norms no longer apply. It would also turn an English reading test into a test of something else.
The NYSESLAT measures English language proficiency; it is not designed to diagnose a reading disability. A sound evaluation uses multiple measures, including assessment in the home language.

questions.key: Norm-referenced scores are valid only for students like the norm group; English-only norms cannot diagnose an ELL's disability.

questions.stem: A grade 11 ELL whose home language is Bengali will take a Regents science exam and the Regents ELA exam in June. Which testing accommodation is available to her on the science exam but unavailable on the ELA exam?
options: Testing with extended time, such as time and a half
Testing in a separate location or in a small group
Using a word-to-word English–Bengali bilingual glossary
Having a staff member explain test questions in Bengali
questions.why: Some ELL accommodations, such as extended time and a separate location, apply to every state test. Bilingual glossaries, translated editions, oral translation, and home-language responses apply to content tests such as math, science, and social studies; none of the translation or glossary supports apply to ELA tests, because those tests measure English itself. No state test permits anyone to explain the questions; even oral translation must translate without clarifying.

traps.note: Extended time is a real ELL accommodation, but it is available on both exams, so it doesn't answer the question about what differs between them.
A separate location is a correct ELL accommodation, but like extended time it applies to all state tests, including ELA, so it isn't the distinction the question asks about.

No state test, science or ELA, allows anyone to explain or clarify the questions. Oral translation, where permitted on content tests, translates the test without explaining it, so this support is unavailable on both exams.

questions.key: Glossaries and translations: content tests only, never ELA. Extended time and a separate location: all state tests.

questions.stem: To prepare a grade 7 ELL for the state math test, the ENL teacher creates an English–Arabic glossary of math terms. Each entry gives the Arabic equivalent, a short definition in Arabic, and a small diagram. Which statement about using this glossary on the state test is accurate?
options: It may be used, since bilingual glossaries are an approved accommodation for ELLs on state math tests.
It may not be used as designed, since approved glossaries give only word-to-word translations, without definitions.
It may be used, provided that the student's IEP lists a bilingual glossary among the testing accommodations.
It may not be used, since bilingual glossaries are permitted on the ELA test, where vocabulary is assessed.
questions.why: Bilingual glossaries are an approved ELL accommodation on content tests (math, science, social studies), but they must be word-to-word: the English term and its home-language equivalent, with no definitions or explanations. A glossary with definitions and diagrams gives students content information that other test takers don't have, so it goes beyond an accommodation. Building a compliant word-to-word glossary, and using it in class, is the right preparation.

traps.note: Glossaries are approved on math tests, but only word-to-word glossaries. This one includes definitions and diagrams, which go beyond translation into content help.
ELL testing accommodations are based on ELL (or former-ELL) status, not on an IEP. An IEP governs disability-related accommodations.
This reverses the rule. Glossaries are allowed on content tests and never on ELA tests, because ELA tests measure English vocabulary and reading.

questions.key: State-test bilingual glossaries are word-to-word only (no definitions or explanations) and are used only on content tests.

questions.stimulus:
Grade 6 Integrated ENL social studies: exit ticket on the objective 'Explain causes and effects of trade along the Silk Road, citing evidence'
Student | NYSESLAT level | Exit-ticket evidence
Ahmad (Pashto) | Entering | Matched causes to effects correctly with picture cards; wrote no sentences
Mei (Mandarin) | Emerging | Matched correctly; wrote 'Silk Road trade. China rich.'
José (Spanish) | Transitioning | Explained one cause correctly using 'because'; cited no evidence
Anya (Ukrainian) | Expanding | Explained two causes with evidence, using 'as a result' and 'therefore'
questions.stem: Which plan for the next lesson makes the best use of these data?
options: Reteach the whole lesson to all four students with simpler texts, so that everyone reaches the same basic understanding first
Give Ahmad and Mei a lower-grade text on a different topic, while José and Anya continue working with the grade-level text
Keep the groups formed in September by NYSESLAT level and continue as planned, since the exit tickets mostly confirm those levels
Group Ahmad and Mei for oral rehearsal with visuals and frames, coach José on citing evidence, and extend Anya, on the same objective
questions.why: Data-driven differentiation means using current evidence to target each student's next step while keeping everyone on the same grade-level objective. Ahmad and Mei understand the cause-and-effect relationships (they matched correctly) but need oral rehearsal and frames to put them into words; José's next step is citing evidence; and Anya has met the objective and needs extension. Because the content understanding is already there, lowering the text or changing the topic is unnecessary.

traps.note: The data show four different next steps, and two students have already shown content understanding. Reteaching everything to everyone with simpler texts ignores that evidence and lowers rigor.

Ahmad and Mei matched causes and effects correctly, so they understand the content. Moving them to a lower-grade text on another topic removes them from grade-level learning they can access with language scaffolds.
NYSESLAT levels are a reasonable starting point, but the exit tickets reveal specific needs (José needs to cite evidence; Anya has met the objective) that fixed level-based groups would ignore.

questions.key: Group flexibly by what current data show each student needs next, while keeping the same grade-level objective for all.

questions.stem: A grade 8 ELL from Senegal whose home language is Wolof will take the Grade 8 state math test. No translated edition of the test is available in Wolof. Which accommodation plan is most consistent with NYS policy?
options: Extended time and a separate location, but no home-language support, since that support requires a state translated edition
Oral translation of the test by a qualified translator, along with extended time and testing in a separate location
Written responses in Wolof, with test items presented in English, since oral translation is permitted only on ELA tests
Seating beside a Wolof-speaking classmate who can explain any test questions the student finds confusing as she works
questions.why: For lower-incidence languages that have no translated edition, NYS permits oral translation of math, science, and social studies tests, and it can be combined with other ELL accommodations such as extended time and a separate location. The translator translates the test but does not explain or clarify its content. Together, these supports keep the test a measure of math rather than of English.

traps.note: Extended time and a separate location are appropriate, but NYS also permits oral translation for lower-incidence languages that have no translated edition, so denying home-language support is incorrect.
This reverses the rules. Oral translation is permitted on math, science, and social studies tests, while translation supports never apply to ELA tests.
A classmate is not a qualified translator, and explaining questions goes beyond translation. It gives help that changes what the test measures and breaks standardized administration.

questions.key: No translated edition? NYS permits oral translation of content tests for lower-incidence languages, together with other ELL accommodations.

questions.stem: A grade 8 ELL at the Emerging level, who attended school through grade 6 in the Dominican Republic, is taking the state science test. Which statement about her written responses is accurate?
options: She may write her responses in Spanish, since ELLs may answer in the home language on content tests.
She needs to write her responses in English, since constructed responses on state tests are scored in English.
She may write in Spanish on the ELA test, where writing is assessed, but not on the science test.
She may write her responses in Spanish, but those answers can earn no more than half of the available credit.
questions.why: On content tests (math, science, social studies), ELLs may write their responses in their home language, and those responses are scored for content. This accommodation is especially valuable for a student with strong prior schooling in Spanish, because it lets her show science knowledge she cannot yet fully express in English. Translation and home-language supports do not apply to ELA tests, which measure English.

traps.note: NYS permits ELLs to write responses to content-test items in the home language. Requiring English would make the science score partly a measure of English writing.
This reverses the rule: home-language responses are allowed on content tests, not on ELA tests, which measure English.
Penalizing home-language answers would make the score reflect language rather than science knowledge, defeating the purpose of the accommodation.

questions.key: On content tests, ELLs may write responses in the home language; this accommodation does not apply to ELA tests.

questions.stem: A student exited ELL status at the end of grade 9 by scoring Commanding on the NYSESLAT. In June of grade 10, she will take the Regents exam in Global History and Geography. Which statement about her testing accommodations is accurate?
options: She may not receive ELL testing accommodations, since those accommodations end when a student exits ELL status.
She may receive ELL testing accommodations, provided that they are written into an IEP or a Section 504 plan.
She may receive extended time, but translated editions and glossaries are reserved for students who are current ELLs.
She may receive ELL testing accommodations, since former ELLs remain eligible for them for two years after exiting.
questions.why: In NYS, former ELLs keep ELL testing accommodations for two years after they exit: extended time, a separate location, word-to-word glossaries, translated editions or oral translation, and home-language responses on content tests. These are ELL accommodations, not disability accommodations, so no IEP or 504 plan is needed. She exited at the end of grade 9, so a June grade 10 Regents exam falls within the two-year window.

traps.note: Exiting does not end testing supports right away. Former ELLs keep ELL testing accommodations for two years after exit.
ELL testing accommodations come from ELL or former-ELL status, not from a disability plan. No IEP or 504 plan is needed.
Former ELLs are eligible for the full set of ELL testing accommodations, not just extended time. Glossaries and translated editions are part of that set on content tests like Global History.

questions.key: Former ELLs keep ELL testing accommodations for two years after exit; no IEP or 504 plan is needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why NYS does not permit bilingual glossaries or translated editions on ELA tests, even though it permits them on math, science, and social studies tests?
options: ELA tests measure English reading and writing, so translation supports would change what the tests are designed to measure.
Translated ELA tests could not be made equal in difficulty across languages, so their scores would not be comparable to English ones.
ELLs are exempt from ELA tests until they reach the Expanding level, so translated supports for ELA tests are not needed.
Glossaries give ELLs an advantage over native English speakers, so NYS limits their use to as few state tests as possible.
questions.why: An accommodation is valid when it removes a barrier unrelated to the construct without changing what is measured. On a science test, English is a barrier to showing science knowledge, so glossaries and translations make the scores more valid. On an ELA test, English reading and writing are the construct, so translating would measure something else entirely. That is why none of the translation or glossary supports apply to ELA tests.

traps.note: Comparability across languages is a real concern for any translated test, yet NYS still offers translated math, science, and social studies tests. So it cannot be the main reason; the main reason is that English is the very construct an ELA test measures.
ELLs take ELA tests. The one exception is a one-time exemption from the Grades 3–8 ELA test in a student's first year in U.S. schools.
Accommodations remove barriers unrelated to the construct, which makes content scores more valid; they do not give an advantage. On content tests, glossaries level access to the content.

questions.key: Accommodations may not change the construct. ELA tests measure English, so translations and glossaries are not permitted on them.

questions.stem: An ENL teacher learns that a grade 4 ELL whose home language is Haitian Creole will use a word-to-word bilingual glossary on the spring state math test. What is the best way for the teacher to prepare the student?
options: Introduce the glossary during the week before the test, so it seems new and helpful when the student uses it on test day
Discourage glossary use in class during the year, so that the student learns to rely on English alone by test day
Provide a full bilingual dictionary in class, since it gives the student more information than the test glossary does
Build regular use of a word-to-word glossary into math lessons and classroom tests throughout the school year
questions.why: Accommodations work best when students have used them routinely during instruction and classroom assessment, so they know how and when the tool helps. Using the same kind of word-to-word glossary in class all year prepares the student to use it efficiently under test conditions. Classroom supports and testing accommodations should match.

traps.note: Introducing it at the last minute gives the student no practice with a new tool under time pressure. Accommodations help most when students have used them routinely.
Discouraging home-language tools treats the home language as a crutch. It also leaves the student unpracticed with an accommodation she is entitled to.
A dictionary with definitions is not what the state test allows, so practicing with it doesn't prepare the student to use the permitted tool efficiently.

questions.key: Practice testing accommodations routinely in class so that students can use them effectively on state tests.

questions.stimulus:
Student profile: Valeria, grade 7
Home language: Spanish (spoken at home)
Schooling: all in NYS schools since kindergarten; all math instruction in English
Spanish literacy: limited; reads simple texts slowly
NYSESLAT: Expanding
questions.stem: The school is planning Valeria's ELL accommodations for the Grade 7 state math test. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Provide the Spanish translated edition, since a translated edition is the most effective accommodation for a Spanish-speaking ELL
Provide no ELL accommodations, since students at the Expanding level are no longer eligible for ELL testing accommodations
Provide the English edition with extended time and a separate location, since she learned math in English and reads Spanish slowly
Provide every available ELL accommodation, including the Spanish edition, so that she has as much support as she could need
questions.why: Accommodations should be chosen for the individual student, based on her proficiency, home-language literacy, and language of instruction. A translated edition helps a student who reads the home language well and learned the content in it, but Valeria learned math in English and reads Spanish slowly. Extended time and a separate location support her access to the English test without adding an unfamiliar reading load.

traps.note: A translated edition helps students who read the home language well and learned the content in it. Valeria learned math in English and reads Spanish slowly, so a Spanish edition would add a reading burden.
All current ELLs, including those at Expanding, are eligible for ELL testing accommodations, and former ELLs remain eligible for two years after exit.
More is not automatically better. Accommodations should fit the individual, and unnecessary materials, such as a test edition in a language she reads slowly, can add load and distraction.

questions.key: Match accommodations to the student: translated editions help students literate in the home language who learned the content in it.

questions.stimulus:
Item analysis: grade 7 science unit test, ELLs at the Transitioning and Expanding levels (9 students)
Item type | Example | ELLs correct
Identify | 'Label the parts of the cell.' | 89%
Describe | 'Describe the function of the cell membrane.' | 78%
Compare/contrast | 'How are plant and animal cells alike and different?' | 33%
Explain cause/effect | 'What happens to a cell if it loses water?' | 74%
Follow-up: When asked orally, most of these students pointed to and named differences between plant and animal cell diagrams.
questions.stem: Based on these results, which instructional response is most appropriate?
options: Reteach the content of the whole cell unit, since the ELLs' overall results show they did not master the material
Teach the language of comparison, such as 'both,' 'whereas,' and 'unlike,' with frames and Venn diagrams in upcoming lessons
Remove compare/contrast items from future tests for ELLs, since this item type does not fairly measure their learning
Assign extra flashcard practice on cell vocabulary, since unfamiliar science terms caused the low scores on these items
questions.why: The ELLs did well on items asking them to identify, describe, and explain cause and effect, but poorly on compare/contrast, and the oral follow-up shows they know the content. That points to a specific language function, not missing content or vocabulary. The data-driven response is targeted instruction in the language of comparison (signal words, frames, graphic organizers) within upcoming science content.

traps.note: The ELLs did well on three of four item types, and the oral follow-up shows they know the differences. Reteaching all the content ignores the specific pattern in the data.
Comparing and contrasting is a grade-level academic language function that students need. Removing it lowers expectations; the data call for teaching it.
Students labeled cell parts correctly, so vocabulary is not the gap. Isolated flashcards also wouldn't teach how to express similarities and differences.

questions.key: Item analysis by language function can reveal a specific language need to teach explicitly within content lessons.

questions.stem: A grade 3 Integrated ENL class is writing opinion pieces about whether the school should plant a garden. The ENL teacher is planning supports for three ELLs at the Entering, Transitioning, and Expanding levels. Which plan best reflects differentiation by proficiency level?
options: All three students complete the same task with the same sentence frames, so that expectations are equal for everyone
The Entering student draws a picture of a garden while the others write, since stating opinions is beyond that level
All three write opinion pieces, with supports that decrease from visuals, a word bank, and frames to a brief checklist
The Entering and Transitioning students copy a model opinion paragraph while the Expanding student writes an original one
questions.why: Differentiating by proficiency level means keeping the same grade-level task and standard while adjusting the amount and type of scaffolding: substantial for Entering (visuals, word banks, frames, home-language support), moderate for Transitioning, and light for Expanding (for example, a checklist). This mirrors the New Language Arts Progressions, in which scaffolding decreases from Entering to Commanding.

traps.note: Equal expectations don't require identical supports. The same frames may be too much for the Expanding student and too little for the Entering student.
Entering students can state opinions in writing with substantial scaffolds (visuals, word banks, frames, home-language support). Drawing alone removes the writing standard.
Copying a model involves no original thinking or language production. Both students can produce their own opinions with level-appropriate scaffolds.

questions.key: Give all students the same grade-level task; scaffolds decrease as proficiency rises, from substantial at Entering to light at Expanding.

questions.stem: An ENL teacher and a grade 6 social studies teacher are reviewing supports for ELLs on an end-of-unit test that asks students to write an argument using two primary sources. Which change would be a modification that alters what the test measures, rather than an accommodation?
options: Allowing extra time to complete the test in a small-group setting
Providing a word-to-word glossary of key social studies terms
Allowing students to write their arguments in the home language
Replacing the argument task with a matching quiz on vocabulary
questions.why: An accommodation changes how a student accesses or responds to an assessment (time, setting, language supports) while keeping the same construct and standard. A modification changes what is measured or lowers the standard; replacing a document-based argument with a vocabulary matching quiz measures something different and far less demanding. For ELLs, the goal is accommodations that preserve grade-level expectations.

traps.note: Extra time and a small-group setting change how the test is given, not what it measures. Students still write the same argument from the same sources.
A word-to-word glossary removes a vocabulary barrier without changing the task or the standard, which makes it an accommodation.
On a social studies test, the construct is historical argument, not English writing. Home-language responses change how students respond, not what is measured.

questions.key: Accommodations change how students access or respond; modifications change what is measured or lower the standard.

questions.stimulus:
Newcomer profile: Nodira, grade 6, home language Uzbek, arrived two months ago
Prior schooling: continuous in Uzbekistan through grade 5
Math assessment in Uzbek (given with an interpreter): grade-level work on fractions, ratios, and multi-step problems
NYSITELL: Entering
Class observation: completes computation quickly and accurately; does not yet understand English word problems
questions.stem: Which decision about Nodira's math instruction makes the best use of these data?
options: Keep her in grade-level math with ENL support, visuals, and home-language resources so she can build on what she knows
Place her in a lower-grade math class until her English improves, so that the language of grade 6 lessons does not overwhelm her
Have her complete computation worksheets during math lessons, since she can work on them independently without needing English
Reassess her math skills with the English grade 6 unit test, since that will show what she can do in her current math class
questions.why: Data from a home-language assessment are often the most valid picture of a newcomer's content knowledge. Nodira's math is on grade level, so her need is language, not math. Keeping her in grade-level math with ENL support, visuals, and home-language resources (such as a bilingual glossary or materials in Uzbek) lets her apply and build on that knowledge while she learns the language of word problems.

traps.note: Her home-language assessment shows grade-level math. Placing her below grade level because of English denies her appropriate content and wastes what she already knows.
Computation she has already mastered keeps her busy but stops her math growth and cuts her off from the class's grade-level problem solving and language.
An English-only test would measure her English, not her math, and the home-language assessment already gives valid evidence of her math knowledge.

questions.key: When home-language data show grade-level content knowledge, keep the newcomer in grade-level content with language supports.

questions.stem: A grade 4 Integrated ENL co-teaching team taught a two-week unit on writing informative paragraphs. On the post-assessment, three Emerging ELLs did not meet the target.
